summary: Postmortem-style technical deep dive on chronic GPU OOMs and intermittent CUDA timeouts observed during customer POC. Explored KV-cache interactions, batching-induced memory spikes, quantization artifacts, NCCL/allreduce issues on multi-GPU, and current retry semantics. Agreement to collect flamegraphs + cuda-memcheck and run deterministic repros in private VPC. Next steps and owners listed.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 47 minutes
Recording: auto
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nanda (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood Infra), Riley Chen (Redwood SRE), Miguel Santos (Aurelia ML), Priya Kapoor (Aurelia Cloud), Elena Morris (Aurelia CTO), Omar Idris (Aurelia Platform)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): frequent OOMs during long-context batched inferencing; CUDA timeouts reported on multi-GPU nodes; apparent correlation with KV cache warmups and long tail sequences; retry policy currently retries on 5xx up to 2x with fixed delay; need deterministic repro and kernel-level traces.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: all right folks let's get started, thank you for joining on a Tuesday. We wanted to run through the postmortem for the OOMs you saw last week and, uh, figure out a path to a deterministic repro.
[00:17] Miguel Santos: thanks. Quick context: we run a mix of short chat queries and long medical note summaries, some requests hit 8k sequence length. We started seeing GPU OOMs on 4/8 GPU nodes, sometimes only one GPU would OOM, sometimes the whole job fails with a timeout.
[00:33] Priya Nanda: when you say OOMs is that CUDA OOM from the process or out-of-memory in the runtime scheduler? Do you have the error msgs?
[00:42] Miguel Santos: we have snippets, here's one from the agent: "RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 1.2 GiB (GPU 0; 47.8 GiB total capacity)" and then a follow-up: "CUDA error: unspecified launch failure"—the logs are a bit noisy.
[00:56] Priya Kapoor: also, side note, we use a VPC-provisioned private cluster and attach to your Dedicated pool via private peering, so network issues shouldn't be contributing but we keep it in mind.
[01:12] Riley Chen: from an SRE side we saw timeouts reported as "CUDA kernel timeout" and the runtime retried the request up to two times, then surfaced a 503 to the app. So the client sees intermittent 5xx.
[01:27] Samir Patel: do you run KV cache (prefix cache) across requests? sometimes warmup leads to large kv allocations per-sequence, especially if keys are stored uncompressed.
[01:40] Miguel Santos: yes, KV cache enabled. We also were using dynamic batching with max_batch_size 64 and a batching timeout of 20ms. But workloads are very skewed: a few requests have seq_len 8k, most are 128.
[01:56] Jordan Lee: okay that's a common pattern—skewed tail sequences plus batching can cause memory blowups because the runtime pads to the longest sequence in a batch unless prefix cache handles it. Do you have the per-request sequence length histogram?
[02:12] Miguel Santos: I sent a csv earlier in the thread, but quick numbers: p95 is 3k, p99 is 7.9k, p999 is 8.2k.
[02:21] Priya Nanda: that explains it. The runtime currently keeps KV cache as a per-request allocation on the GPU in our Dedicated mode; when you batch a 128 and an 8k request, the 8k drives memory for all. We do some streaming to avoid full allocation but with our current kernel choice it still needs significant memory.
[02:39] Miguel Santos: got it. We also noticed that on multi-GPU jobs the OOMs sometimes come from NCCL/allreduce when we're sharded across GPUs. Error looked like "NCCL WARN Call to cudaLaunchKernel failed with error 700"
[02:53] Riley Chen: NCCL error 700 is basically a device-side assert/timeout. That can be triggered by a kernel taking too long or a preceding OOM.
[03:05] Priya Kapoor: is it possible that quantization is introducing instability? we're running int8 quant on some models in the POC to save memory.
[03:13] Samir Patel: quant + fused kernels sometimes changes kernel occupancy and register pressure which can increase runtime kernel duration—combined with long sequences and high batch sizes it could flip a kernel over the driver watchdog threshold, causing a CUDA timeout and then an NCCL abort.
[03:29] Jordan Lee: yes, and our retry semantics currently treat kernel timeouts as retryable once, then escalate. But if the kernel leaves the GPU in a bad state, subsequent retries on same node can also fail. That's why we have backoff + node blacklisting in the Dedicated scheduler, but it only kicks in after 2 failures.
[03:45] Miguel Santos: that resonates—some of our traces show two quick retries then an immediate job failure.
[03:52] Priya Nanda: we need a few diagnostics: 1) per-request GPU memory timeline (alloc/free) 2) cuda-memcheck and nvprof traces for failing requests 3) full scheduler logs with which GPU device handled which micro-batch.
[04:06] Miguel Santos: we can collect those, though cuda-memcheck in production is heavy. We can target a subset traffic.
[04:14] Jordan Lee: agreed run targeted traffic. Also, try disabling KV cache or switching to remote KV (off-GPU) to see if memory pressure drops.
[04:24] Omar Idris: just to flag constraints: our infra team won't allow modifications to kernel driver or changing watchdog timers on the host. So any mitigation must be at runtime or config level.
[04:35] Priya Nanda: good to note. We'll avoid host-level changes.
[04:40] [05:00] Jordan Lee: walk through a concrete repro plan—Priya, Samir, you take lead from Redwood side.
[05:06] Priya Nanda: step one: reproduce on a small dedicated instance in the customer's VPC with exact batch profile. We'll enable verbose mem-trace logging for 200 requests then pull GPU traces. Step two: flip quantization to fp16 for the failing model to compare. Step three: run with KV cache disabled and with KV offloaded to host memory.
[05:24] Miguel Santos: question on offload: how much perf hit do you expect if we move KV to host? Our latency p95 budget is 300ms for short queries, but for long sequences we can tolerate more.
[05:36] Samir Patel: rough rule: offload adds ~20-40ms per request for KV fetchs for mid-length; for 8k sequences it can help because you avoid a 10+ GB allocation on GPU, so net latency might improve if OOMs are avoided.
[05:52] Priya Kapoor: can fallback to smaller batch sizes for long tail? like dynamic batch capping at 8 for seq>2k?
[06:00] Riley Chen: yes that's a proven mitigation—batch cap plus sequence-length aware batching (bucketed batching). We can implement an admission policy to prevent long-seq from combining with short-seq.
[06:12] Elena Morris: one other item: our workload uses mixed request types and we can't easily pre-bucket in the app. Is there a runtime-level feature to do that?
[06:22] Priya Nanda: we're working on sequence-aware batching in the runtime where we pre-bucket by an approximate sequence-length estimate from the metadata. We can add a temporary config for you to enable bucketed batching in Dedicated.
[06:34] Miguel Santos: about retries — we saw duplicate processing of side-effects because our upstream job is not idempotent. Retries cause double writes. Can Redwood support idempotency keys or better retry routing?
[06:46] Jordan Lee: we have request-id passthrough in the API, but the runtime retry might replay on a different backend; we can propagate an idempotency-key header and stop automatic retries for requests marked non-idempotent. We should add a policy to not retry for any request flagged X-Non-Idempotent.
[07:03] Omar Idris: that's critical for us, yes.
[07:07] Priya Nanda: action item: we'll add a config flag and a patch for the retry logic that respects X-Idempotency-Key and X-Non-Idempotent.
[07:17] Miguel Santos: back to CUDA errors—is there value in running cuda-memcheck for a single problematic request to get exact stack?
[07:24] Samir Patel: yes cuda-memcheck and nvprof plus nvtx markers in the runtime. Also collect the driver logs (dmesg) to see if the watchdog fired. If watchdog fired you often see TDR-like kernel resets.
[07:38] Priya Kapoor: we will need Redwood to gather stack traces — we don't have confidence on how to enable nvtx in your runtime hooks.
[07:46] Priya Nanda: we'll provide a debug build that turns on NVTX ranges around kernel launches and enables verbose allocator logs. That build will be safe for a small test window.
[07:57] Miguel Santos: regarding NCCL errors — could multi-GPU sharding be a contributing factor? we saw that single GPU jobs sometimes succeed but sharded jobs fail.
[08:08] Riley Chen: multi-GPU increases surface area. NCCL will synchronize kernels and if one GPU hits a timeout other peers will hang. We need to check whether memory fragmentation on one device caused the initial OOM which then cascaded. Also check cudaGraph usage if any—graphs can pin memory.
[08:26] Jordan Lee: any telemetry where we see per-GPU memory fragmentation metrics?
[08:30] Samir Patel: runtime doesn't currently emit fragmentation metrics by default but we can enable histogram of free-block sizes and external fragmentation ratio for the debug window.
[08:41] Miguel Santos: can you explain the kernel watchdog threshold? we've got tuned kernels that sometimes spike in runtime.
[08:47] Priya Nanda: watchdog kicks in when a kernel runs longer than the driver's max kernel time (on Linux X it's typically a few seconds for display drivers; on data-center drivers it's often disabled but some hosts enforce a watchdog). If quantization or fused ops increase per-token kernel time, you can exceed that. We can look at per-kernel latencies in nvprof.
[09:05] Elena Morris: OK, next I want to call out an intermittent "unspecified launch failure" we saw in logs earlier. Any idea what that points to?
[09:12] Samir Patel: "unspecified launch failure" is generic; most often it's a device-side assert or illegal memory access during a kernel. That can happen if memory is corrupted—rare but possible with certain fused kernels or driver/compatibility bugs. We'll check GPU driver versions and the exact compute capability interplay with the quantized kernels.
[09:30] Jordan Lee: on the compatibility note, what driver and CUDA versions are you on?
[09:34] Priya Kapoor: running CUDA 12.2 drivers, NVIDIA driver 545.x, nodes are A100 40GB.
[09:41] Priya Nanda: A100 40GB with CUDA 12.2 is reasonable. We'll check kernel builds against that target. Some quant kernels were tuned for 12.1 and could be slightly off.
[09:49] Miguel Santos: is there a recommended memory safety config? like soft-limits per-model or per-request?
[09:55] Riley Chen: yes we can set per-model memory caps and an eviction policy for KV cache—evict least-recently-used prefixes when memory high. Also per-request max-kv-size.
[10:06] Jordan Lee: another option: enable continuous batching with KV sharing—if requests share prefixes we can reuse same KV instead of allocating twice. That only helps if prefix similarity is high.
[10:18] Miguel Santos: our clinical notes often share a lot of tokens in repeating headers, so that could help.
[10:23] Priya Nanda: let's outline immediate mitigations: 1) cap batch size for long sequences 2) enable bucketed batching 3) offload KV to host for long seqs 4) disable int8 for the failing model while we debug 5) add idempotency header handling for retries 6) collect kernel-level traces.
[10:44] Elena Morris: sounds good. Any thoughts on long-term: are there runtime-level compilation changes to avoid big allocations?
[10:51] Samir Patel: compilation-level: use streaming KV layout to allocate KV in smaller chunks, enable chunked attention kernels, and choose kernels favoring lower peak memory even if they cost extra compute. Also adopt memory defragmentation passes in allocator.
[11:08] Jordan Lee: and on the scheduler: we can incorporate sequence-length-aware scheduling so long sequences are isolated to dedicated nodes with higher memory headroom. That could be part of Dedicated plan.
[11:20] Miguel Santos: last technical question: we saw OOMs concentrated at high-concurrency times. Is there a safe admission control you recommend?
[11:28] Riley Chen: yes simple token-concurrency cap: limit number of concurrent long-seq in flight per-GPU; if exceeded either reject with 429 or route to a lower-priority pool. We can add exponential backoff responses to reduce thundering.
[11:44] Jordan Lee: we should also talk about metrics we'll collect for the follow-up: per-request alloc_peak, per-kernel time, nvml GPU memory deltas, orphaned allocations, and scheduler decision logs.
[11:58] Priya Kapoor: we'll grant access to the cluster logs temporarily for Redwood debug account.
[12:05] Miguel Santos: about the duplication issue—will the runtime include request-id mapping in the logs so we can correlate application-level writes to specific requests?
[12:14] Priya Nanda: yes, we'll add request-id in the allocator and kernel nvtx ranges so traces can be tied back to request id.
[12:24] [12:30] Jordan Lee: ok let's recap and agree owners—then open the debug window.
[12:33] Jordan Lee: recap: Redwood provides debug build + NVTX hooks (Priya Nanda), collect cuda-memcheck traces (Miguel), run repro with KV offload and fp16 toggle (Miguel), implement idempotency-aware retry flag (Samir), propose scheduler and batch cap patches (Riley/Samir). We'll sync in a week.
[12:54] Miguel Santos: one more minor transcription / observation: sometimes the transcribed logs show "K V cash" instead of KV cache in our logs, just noting the auto-transcription is messy.
[13:05] Priya Nanda: haha noted. We'll annotate artifacts we share so transcripts match.
[13:10] Jordan Lee: any final Qs?
[13:12] Elena Morris: no, thanks everyone.
[13:14] Jordan Lee: thanks, meeting adjourned.
